content: Many sex workers have transitioned to alternative income-generating activities and have ceased engaging in sex work. A significant number of sex workers report consistent condom use and practicing safe sex, which they attribute to behavior change programs. In Nigeria, national laws criminalize sex work, creating substantial barriers to providing services to this population. Sex workers have emphasized the importance of building trust with EFMC staff, as many have previously encountered negative experiences with other program staff and healthcare services. In Mozambique, Jhpiego, with funding from PEPFAR and in collaboration with the CDC, has supported the government’s HIV prevention programs, including the Voluntary Medical Male Circumcision (VMMC) program and homeand community-based HIV Testing Services (HTS). The HTS program employs lay counselors, referred to as community counselors, who are recruited from local community and faith-based groups. Home-based HTS has been well-received in Mozambican communities, with over one million clients tested between 2007 and 2014. Over time, the role of community counselors has expanded to include additional health screenings and education, such as measuring blood pressure to screen for hypertension. Community counselors actively follow up with individuals (e.g., those with suspected TB, pregnant women without antenatal care, victims of gender-based violence) to ensure they receive necessary care. The Mozambican VMMC program, initiated in November 2009, had reached 322,129 men by February 2015. As the number and capacity of VMMC sites grew in 2012, community counselors were trained to refer HIV-negative men identified through HTS to VMMC services. To enhance their credibility, community counselors underwent VMMC counseling training and a two-week internship at VMMC sites, where they observed client flow from group education to post-operative follow-up. Approximately 8% of men linked to VMMC sites received circumcision services. In Kenya, LVCT Health launched a key population program in 2004 to address the sexual and reproductive health needs of men who have sex with men (MSM) and sex workers. These groups traditionally face limited access to healthcare due to criminalization and stigmatization. The program was developed in collaboration with MSM and sex workers, ensuring services were tailored to their needs. The program offers a comprehensive package of HIV services, with outreach HTS serving as the entry point to other STI and sexual reproductive health services. Trained peer educators provide psychosocial support and follow-up for newly diagnosed clients to promote treatment adherence and retention. Additional services include STI testing and treatment, cervical cancer screening, post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for HIV-negative individuals, condom distribution, and linkage to care and treatment for HIV-positive clients. Peer educators identify locations frequented by MSM and sex workers, mobilize the community, and create demand for HTS. Gatekeepers, such as brothel and bar security guards, are sensitized to the health needs of these populations. Clients testing HIV-negative receive information on prevention interventions and access to services. Continuous on-the-job training and mentorship are provided to peer providers and healthcare workers to maintain service quality. From 2011 to 2014, over 4,058 MSM and 4,231 female sex workers accessed integrated HIV prevention, treatment, care, and sexual and reproductive health services. Among these, 1,668 MSM and 2,269 female sex workers underwent HIV testing for the first time. During this period, 650 MSM and 254 sex workers were diagnosed as HIV-positive, with over 75% effectively linked to treatment. Of these, 164 HIV-positive MSM enrolled in LVCT clinics and initiated antiretroviral therapy, achieving a 95% treatment adherence rate and 90% viral suppression among retained clients. In South Africa, the International Center for AIDS Care and Treatment Programs (ICAP) at Columbia University launched the MOSAIC Men’s Health Initiative in 2012. This program aimed to improve access, coverage, and quality of HIV prevention services for MSM. MOSAIC supports MSM organizations in developing peer-led outreach and community-based HIV prevention activities. Services include HTS (via mobile services, couples testing, and home-based testing), STI and TB screening with referrals for treatment, substance abuse and mental health referrals, condom and lubricant distribution, PEP referrals, and linkage to care and treatment for HIV-positive MSM. The program incorporates a monitoring and evaluation framework to track performance and address gaps. Capacity-building initiatives sensitize healthcare workers to the needs of MSM, ensuring sustainability of HIV prevention services. Between 2012 and February 2015, 13,980 MSM received HIV prevention services, 2,010 healthcare workers underwent sensitivity training, and 269 clinicians received clinical training. In Zimbabwe, the Organization for Public Health Interventions and Development (OPHID) introduced a play center project in 2008 as part of PMTCT programs to support vulnerable children in rural districts. By 2011, 176 community volunteers staffed 16 play centers, enrolling 697 children. Following enrollment, 90% of children were up-to-date on immunizations, and improvements in growth, physical strength, confidence, and social interaction were reported. However, only 59% of children were tested for HIV due to the requirement for caregiver consent. All HIV-positive children were successfully linked to treatment, and standardized registers helped prevent loss to follow-up. In Rwanda, Heineken Breweries partnered with PharmAccess International Foundation in 2001 to launch the Heineken Access to HAART Program, providing comprehensive HIV prevention and treatment services to employees and their dependents. The program guarantees lifelong treatment for HIV-positive individuals, even if they are laid off. By January 2005, 736 individuals had received HTS, identifying 109 HIV-positive cases. The program has reduced stigma and increased participation as employees observe successful treatment outcomes and Heineken’s commitment to non-discrimination. In Uganda, modern quality improvement approaches have been implemented to enhance linkage and enrollment from HTS to care and treatment. Interventions such as same-day enrollment in care and peer escorts to ART clinics significantly improved linkage rates, increasing from 58% in August 2013 to 89% in April 2014. Reproductive Health Uganda (RHU) also launched a peer-led program in Kampala’s urban slums to provide SRH and HIV services to sex workers. Services include STI management, family planning, substance use counseling, condom distribution, and referrals for PEP and HIV care. Ninety peer educators were trained to mobilize the community and provide referrals, ensuring comprehensive service delivery.
